title: A snack melting in his pocket led Percy Spencer to the microwave oven

cover.alt: Percy Spencer, a bald engineer in round glasses, grins as popcorn bursts into the air in front of a copper magnetron in a 1940s laboratory.

body: In 1945 **Percy Spencer**, an engineer at Raytheon in Waltham, Massachusetts, was working with magnetrons, the tubes that made the microwaves for radar, when a snack bar in his pocket melted. The earliest account, from 1958, calls it a peanut bar. He sent for some popcorn, which popped all over the lab, and the next morning he tried an egg in a kettle, which exploded in the face of a sceptical engineer. Raytheon filed his patent for cooking with microwaves in October 1945, and in 1947 sold the first Radarange: a water-cooled cabinet nearly 6 feet tall that weighed about 750 pounds, made for commercial kitchens, not homes. Affordable countertop models came in 1967.

slides.alt: A 1940s laboratory with a copper magnetron on the bench. Percy Spencer, bald, in round glasses and a suit, stares in shock at the brown goo dripping from his jacket pocket.
slides.caption: Waltham, Massachusetts, 1945. Raytheon engineer Percy Spencer is testing magnetrons, the tubes that power radar, when his snack bar melts.

slides.alt: Popcorn bursts out of a paper bag in front of the magnetron and flies everywhere. A young engineer in shirtsleeves gapes; Spencer grins.
slides.caption: He sends a boy out for popcorn and holds it near the magnetron. It pops all over the lab.

slides.alt: A kettle beside the magnetron bursts open, spraying bits of egg. The engineer who peeked in reels back with egg on his face; Spencer grins.
slides.caption: Next morning: an egg in a kettle with a hole in its side. A sceptical engineer peeks in. The egg explodes.

slides.question: In 1947 Raytheon sold its first microwave oven, the Radarange. About how much did it weigh?
slides.explanation: The 1947 Radarange was a water-cooled cabinet nearly 6 feet tall, made for commercial kitchens. Affordable countertop models came in 1967.

source.label: Percy Spencer, 'Method of treating foodstuffs', US patent 2,495,429
